title: Compound Inequalities
_notes: Source of truth for the 1.5 practice set. Every compound inequality is read by tools/build_exercises.py (comp_set: the solution set as exact intervals, for a single inequality, the three-part form a < x < b, "A and B" and "A or B"), so an open or closed circle, an overlap or a union can never be wrong. Typed answers (kind "num") carry "derive": smallest-int / largest-int, count-int (how many whole numbers solve q) or count-out (how many do not; the gap of an "or") as in 1.4, or first-error. Mistakes "m": smallest/largest-int edge, other, sign; count-int closed, open, gap, inner; count-out edge, gap, neighbors; first-error last, before, after, first. "match" checks: join (and / or), graph (inequality → graph in words, any compound set), same-solution; "multi" checks: solution:<inequality> (numbers that make it true) and valid-from:<inequality>. Chips: ADD, SUBTRACT, MULTIPLY, DIVIDE, DIST, COMBINE as in 1.3; SOLVE (each part of an and / or solved on its own, blue) and LIST (the whole numbers that fit, green). See docs/exercises.md.

exercises.prompt: Match each inequality with the word that joins its two conditions.
exercises.read: Match each inequality with the word that joins its two conditions: and, or or.
exercises.say_answer: And means both at once, so the graph is the overlap. Or means either one, so the graph is both pieces together. The three-part form is an and in disguise.

pairs.why: And means both conditions hold at the same time: the graph is the overlap.
pairs.say: X greater than two and x less than six. And means both at once, so the graph is the overlap.

pairs.why: The three-part form is an and in disguise: x is greater than 2 and less than 6.
pairs.say: Two is less than x, which is less than six. The three-part form is an and in disguise.

pairs.why: Or means either condition is enough: the graph is both pieces together.
pairs.say: X less than two or x greater than six. Or means either one is enough, so the graph is both pieces together.

pairs.why: Or means either condition is enough: the graph is both pieces together.
pairs.say: X less than or equal to negative one, or x greater than or equal to four. Or means either one is enough.

exercises.prompt: Match each compound inequality with its graph.
exercises.read: Match each compound inequality with its graph.
exercises.say_answer: A three-part inequality is shaded between its two circles. An or inequality is two rays that point away from each other. Each circle is closed when its symbol includes equality and open when it does not.

pairs.r: Closed at −2, open at 3, shaded between
pairs.why: The left symbol includes equality, so the circle at −2 is closed. The right one does not, so the circle at 3 is open.
pairs.say: Negative two is less than or equal to x, which is less than three: a closed circle at negative two, an open circle at three, shaded between.

pairs.r: Open at 1, closed at 5, shaded between
pairs.why: The left symbol leaves 1 out, so its circle is open. The right one keeps 5, so its circle is closed.
pairs.say: One is less than x, which is less than or equal to five: an open circle at one, a closed circle at five, shaded between.

pairs.r: Open at −1, shaded left; closed at 2, shaded right
pairs.why: Two rays that point away from each other: open at −1 going left, closed at 2 going right.
pairs.say: X less than negative one, or x greater than or equal to two: an open circle at negative one shaded left, a closed circle at two shaded right.

pairs.r: Closed at 0, shaded left; open at 4, shaded right
pairs.why: Two rays that point away from each other: closed at 0 going left, open at 4 going right.
pairs.say: X less than or equal to zero, or x greater than four: a closed circle at zero shaded left, an open circle at four shaded right.

exercises.prompt: Select all the numbers that are solutions of 2 < x ≤ 8.
exercises.read: Select all the numbers that are solutions of two is less than x, which is less than or equal to eight.
exercises.say_answer: Five and eight are solutions. Two is not, because its circle is open, eight is, because its circle is closed, and nine and zero are outside the graph.

options.why: 2 is not greater than 2: the circle at 2 is open.
options.say: Two. No: two is not greater than two, so the circle at two is open.

options.why: 5 is between 2 and 8.
options.say: Five. Yes: five is between two and eight.

options.why: 8 is less than or equal to 8: the circle at 8 is closed.
options.say: Eight. Yes: eight is less than or equal to eight, so the circle at eight is closed.

options.why: 9 is more than 8, outside the graph.
options.say: Nine. No: nine is more than eight, outside the graph.

options.why: 0 is less than 2, outside the graph.
options.say: Zero. No: zero is less than two, outside the graph.

exercises.prompt: Select all the numbers that are solutions of x < −1 or x ≥ 3.
exercises.read: Select all the numbers that are solutions of x less than negative one, or x greater than or equal to three.
exercises.say_answer: Negative two, three and ten are solutions. Negative one and zero are in the gap between the two rays.

options.why: −1 is not less than −1, and it is not 3 or more.
options.say: Negative one. No: negative one is not less than negative one, and it is not three or more.

options.why: −2 is less than −1.
options.say: Negative two. Yes: negative two is less than negative one.

options.why: 0 is in the gap: it is neither less than −1 nor 3 or more.
options.say: Zero. No: zero is in the gap, neither less than negative one nor three or more.

options.why: 3 is greater than or equal to 3: the circle at 3 is closed.
options.say: Three. Yes: three is greater than or equal to three, so the circle at three is closed.

options.why: 10 is 3 or more.
options.say: Ten. Yes: ten is three or more.

exercises.prompt: How many whole numbers solve it? Type the number.
exercises.read: How many whole numbers solve negative three is less than x, which is less than or equal to four?
say: The circle at negative three is open, so negative three is left out. The circle at four is closed, so four is in. The whole numbers are negative two, negative one, zero, one, two, three and four: seven numbers.

wrong.why: Counting −3 as well gives 8, but the circle at −3 is open, so it is left out.
wrong.say: count both circles as filled in

wrong.why: Leaving 4 out gives 6, but the circle at 4 is closed, so 4 counts.
wrong.say: leave out both end numbers

wrong.why: The distance 4 − (−3) = 7 already skips the open end, so taking 2 more away loses numbers.
wrong.say: take both ends away from the distance

exercises.prompt: Starting from −4 < 2x − 2 ≤ 6, which of these could be the next line? Select all that apply.
exercises.read: Starting from negative four is less than two x minus two, which is less than or equal to six, which of these could be the next line? Choose all that apply.
exercises.say_answer: Three lines follow: negative two is less than two x, which is less than or equal to eight; negative two is less than x minus one, which is less than or equal to three; and negative one is less than x, which is less than or equal to four. Each one keeps the same solutions.

options.why: 2 was added to all three parts.
options.say: Negative two is less than two x, which is less than or equal to eight. Yes: two was added to all three parts.

options.why: All three parts were divided by 2.
options.say: Negative two is less than x minus one, which is less than or equal to three. Yes: all three parts were divided by two.

options.why: Two steps in one: add 2, then divide by 2.
options.say: Negative one is less than x, which is less than or equal to four. Yes: that is two steps in one, add two and then divide by two.

options.why: 2 was subtracted, but the original has − 2, so 2 must be added.
options.say: Negative six is less than two x, which is less than or equal to four. No: two was subtracted, but the work has minus two, so two must be added.

options.why: The right symbol changed from ≤ to <: each end keeps its own symbol.
options.say: Negative two is less than two x, which is less than eight. No: the right symbol changed, but each end keeps its own symbol.

exercises.prompt: Match each inequality with its solution.
exercises.read: Match each inequality with its solution.
exercises.say_answer: Solve each part the way you solve any inequality. An and gives the overlap and an or gives both pieces. Remember to flip the symbol only when you multiply or divide by a negative number.

pairs.why: Add 2 to all three parts: the symbols stay.
pairs.say: Negative five is less than or equal to x minus two, which is less than one. Add two to all three parts: negative three is less than or equal to x, which is less than three.

pairs.why: The first part gives x < 3, the second x > −3: both at once is the overlap.
pairs.say: Two x is less than six and x plus one is greater than negative two. The first part gives x less than three, the second x greater than negative three. Both at once is the overlap.

pairs.why: The first part gives x < −1, the second x > 3: either one is enough.
pairs.say: X plus one is less than zero, or x minus three is greater than zero. The first part gives x less than negative one, the second x greater than three. Either one is enough.

pairs.why: The first part gives x ≥ 2, and the second is already solved: both pieces together.
pairs.say: Three x is greater than or equal to six, or x is less than negative four. The first part gives x greater than or equal to two. Both pieces together.

exercises.prompt: What is the largest whole number that solves it? Type it.
exercises.read: What is the largest whole number that solves three is less than or equal to two x minus one, which is less than eleven?
say: Add one to all three parts, by the addition property. Four is less than or equal to two x, which is less than twelve.
Divide all three parts by two, by the division property. Two is less than or equal to x, which is less than six. Six is not included, so the largest whole number is five.

wrong.why: Six is not a solution: x < 6 leaves it out, because the circle at 6 is open.
wrong.say: include the open end

wrong.why: Two is the smallest solution, from the other end of the graph.
wrong.say: read the wrong end of the graph

wrong.why: The boundaries are positive: the graph runs from 2 to 6.
wrong.say: give the boundaries the wrong sign

exercises.prompt: Which line of the student's work is the first one that is wrong? Type its number: the first line is line 1.
exercises.read: A student's work is on the screen, line one at the top. Which line is the first one that is wrong?
say: Add two to all three parts: negative four plus two is negative two, not negative six. The left part was done wrong, so line two is wrong.
Dividing all three parts by two is fine on its own, but it carries the error.
Writing it with the word and is fine on its own too, but it still carries the error.

wrong.why: Line four is only where the wrong answer shows up. The mistake happened earlier.
wrong.say: point at the final answer

wrong.why: Line three is fine on its own: dividing all three parts by 2 is allowed.
wrong.say: blame the line after the mistake

wrong.why: Line one is the inequality the student was given.
wrong.say: blame the given inequality

exercises.prompt: Select all the numbers that are solutions of −7 < 1 − 2x ≤ 5.
exercises.read: Select all the numbers that are solutions of negative seven is less than one minus two x, which is less than or equal to five.
exercises.say_answer: Negative two, zero and three are solutions: the solutions are negative two less than or equal to x, less than four. Dividing by negative two flips both symbols.

options.say: Negative two. Yes: one minus two times negative two is five, and negative seven is less than five, which is less than or equal to five.
Zero. Yes: one minus two times zero is one, which is between negative seven and five.
Three. Yes: one minus two times three is negative five, which is between negative seven and five.

options.why: 1 − 2(4) = −7, which is not greater than −7.
options.say: Four. No: one minus two times four is negative seven, which is not greater than negative seven.

options.why: 1 − 2(−3) = 7, which is more than 5.
options.say: Negative three. No: one minus two times negative three is seven, which is more than five.

exercises.prompt: How many whole numbers are NOT solutions? Type the number.
exercises.read: How many whole numbers are not solutions of x less than negative two, or x greater than three?
say: The solutions are two rays, and the whole numbers in the gap between them are left out. Both circles are open, so negative two and three are in the gap too: negative two, negative one, zero, one, two and three. That is six numbers.

wrong.why: That would be true if the circles at −2 and 3 were filled in. Both are open, so −2 and 3 are not solutions.
wrong.say: treat the open circles as closed

wrong.why: 3 − (−2) = 5 misses one number: both −2 and 3 are in the gap.
wrong.say: subtract the boundaries

wrong.why: −3 and 4 are solutions, so they do not count.
wrong.say: count the nearest solutions too

exercises.prompt: How many whole numbers solve it? Type the number.
exercises.read: How many whole numbers solve negative six is less than two times the quantity x minus one, which is less than eight?
say: Distribute the two: two times x is two x, and two times negative one is negative two. Negative six is less than two x minus two, which is less than eight.
Add two to all three parts, by the addition property. Negative four is less than two x, which is less than ten.
Divide all three parts by two, by the division property. Negative two is less than x, which is less than five.
Both circles are open, so negative two and five are left out. The whole numbers are negative one, zero, one, two, three and four: six numbers.

wrong.why: Counting −2 and 5 as well gives 8, but both circles are open, so they are left out.
wrong.say: count both circles as filled in

wrong.why: 5 − (−2) = 7 is the distance, not the count: with both ends left out there is one fewer number.
wrong.say: subtract the boundaries

wrong.why: Taking 2 away from the distance 7 removes one number too many.
wrong.say: take both ends away from the distance

exercises.prompt: How many whole numbers are NOT solutions? Type the number.
exercises.read: How many whole numbers are not solutions of x plus four is less than three, or two x minus three is greater than three?
say: Solve each part on its own. X plus four is less than three, so x is less than negative one. Two x minus three is greater than three, so two x is greater than six, and x is greater than three.
The whole numbers in the gap are left out, and both circles are open: negative one, zero, one, two and three. That is five numbers.

wrong.why: That would be true if the circles at −1 and 3 were filled in. Both are open, so −1 and 3 are not solutions.
wrong.say: treat the open circles as closed

wrong.why: 3 − (−1) = 4 misses one number: both −1 and 3 are in the gap.
wrong.say: subtract the boundaries

wrong.why: −2 and 4 are solutions, so they do not count.
wrong.say: count the nearest solutions too

exercises.prompt: Which line of the student's work is the first one that is wrong? Type its number: the first line is line 1.
exercises.q:
2x − 1 < −5 or x + 2 ≥ 6
2x < −4 or x ≥ 4
x < 2 or x ≥ 4
x < 2 or 4 ≤ x
x < 2 or x − 4 ≥ 0
exercises.read: A student's work is on the screen, line one at the top. Which line is the first one that is wrong?
say: Each part is solved on its own: add one to the left part, and subtract two from the right part. Both are allowed, so line two is fine.
Divide negative four by two: the result is negative two, not two. The student dropped the sign, so line three is wrong.
Writing four is less than or equal to x is the same as x greater than or equal to four, so this step is fine on its own, but it carries the error.
Moving the four to the left side is fine on its own too, but it still carries the error.

wrong.why: Line five is only where the wrong answer shows up. The mistake happened earlier.
wrong.say: point at the final answer

wrong.why: Line two is fine: each part was solved correctly.
wrong.say: blame the line before the mistake

wrong.why: Line four is fine on its own: swapping the sides is allowed.
wrong.say: blame the line after the mistake
